extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_short: assessing patent novelty and public use
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent validity defenses focused on prior description/publication, public use or sale before application, disclaimers, and the experimental-use exception. Targets legal analysis of whether prior knowledge or use defeats a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior description must enable the public to practise the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must be such as to give the public the means of knowledge, or, in other words, must of itself enable the public to practise the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary that the invention have been reduced to practice, but unless the description would enable the public, without further invention, to put the thing in practice, it cannot be said that knowledge of that thing is in the public's possession. Mere suggestions or experimental speculations that do not serve as practical directions (e.g., Marquis of Worcester's hints) do not defeat a later patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior publication accessible to the public defeats patent by presumption of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: If a printed description was so printed and published as to be accessible to the public, the presumption is against the patentee, and his patent will be defeated, notwithstanding he may not have seen it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether publication was sufficiently accessible is a question for the jury considering all circumstances of the publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior account must be of a complete and perfect invention published as such
rubrics_metrics.description: An account published as an experiment, suggestion, or speculation (not as a complete, perfected, and successful invention) is not the sort of publication that will vitiate subsequent letters-patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A useful test is whether what was published would itself be the subject of letters-patent; mere experimental suggestions that could not be patented should not defeat a later patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defence of want of novelty for material part known or used before
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant who proves a material part of the invention to have been known or used before the patentee's discovery may succeed in the statute defence of want of novelty, provided the patentee's specification was made broader than his real discovery with wilful default or intent to defraud or mislead the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification was broadened accidentally or through inadvertence, the patent remains good for the bona fide part of the invention that the patentee actually discovered, provided that part is material and definitely distinguishable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect and timing of disclaimers on novelty defence and costs
rubrics_metrics.description: If a disclaimer of the improperly claimed part has been filed in the patent office in reasonable time, a defence of want of novelty that attacks only part of the thing patented will not be a complete answer to an action but will prevent recovery of costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No costs can be recovered unless the plaintiff filed a disclaimer of all the part of the thing patented which the original specification should not have claimed before bringing the action. Unreasonable neglect or delay in entering the disclaimer may permit the defence to be admitted as a bar; unreasonable neglect is a question of law for the court. Notices of defence should specify the particular parts intended to be attacked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use or sale before application may constitute abandonment/dedication
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inventor allowed his invention to become public, or it had been in public use or on sale with his consent or allowance before his application for a patent, this may constitute an abandonment or dedication to the public and bar patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The central question is whether the inventor's acts or acquiescence furnish satisfactory proof of abandonment/dedication; courts have held that voluntary public sale or use before application may vacate patent rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'public use' (use by others or sale for use by others)
rubrics_metrics.description: By 'public use' is meant use in public — e.g., if the inventor makes and sells the thing to be used by others, or it is made by another with his knowledge and without objection, it will be public use. If the patentee alone makes the thing for purposes of experiment and completion without selling it to be used by others, 'public use' is not applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use by the inventor for experiments is not public use. Public use requires more: general allowance or acquiescence, or being effectively unlimited in time, extent, or object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of public use without objection raises presumption of acquiescence
rubrics_metrics.description: A knowledge of such public use or sale by others, without objection on the inventor's part, will go far towards raising the presumption of an acquiescence, and in some cases will be sufficient proof of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If knowledge of the use is 'brought home' to the inventor and no exclusive right is asserted, silence is strong evidence of waiver; long acquiescence or very general use can be conclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge may be presumed from circumstances (no direct proof always required)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although acquiescence cannot be presumed without knowledge, such knowledge may be presumed from the circumstances and is not always required to be proved by direct evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether knowledge may be presumed is generally a question of fact for the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: No fixed lapse of time required after knowledge/acquiescence to show abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: No particular lapse of time is necessary to be shown after knowledge and acquiescence are established in order to prove an abandonment or dedication to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples show varying intervals (months to years) where courts held abandonment based on circumstances rather than a fixed time period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor's intention often immaterial where invention becomes public without assertion
rubrics_metrics.description: The intention of the inventor is not the true ground in these cases; whatever his intention, if he suffers the invention to get into public use through any means whatsoever without an immediate assertion of his right, he is not entitled to a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the invention becomes known to the public through fraudulent means the inventor should assert his right immediately; failure to do so may create presumption of dedication despite initial fraudulent disclosure by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental-use exception (acts to perfect/explain do not create dedication)
rubrics_metrics.description: When acts of use were by way of experiment to perfect the invention, the inventor does not lose his right; experimental practice by the inventor, whether in public or private, is not sufficient to prove dedication unless it appears the use was for gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lending a machine to another for testing or occasional use to discover whether a patent is worth taking out has been held not to constitute public use if limited in purpose, time, and extent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secret construction under injunction or confidentiality is not public use
rubrics_metrics.description: Work done under an injunction of secrecy or confidential disclosure (e.g., making a single pair of wheels under secrecy to be shipped abroad) does not amount to a public use within the realm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure to persons connected with the inventor and acting confidentially (e.g., co-investors, agents) will generally be treated as private, not public, and will not vitiate novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale as an article of commerce for profit constitutes public use
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee before his patent constructed and sold articles as an article of commerce for gain, and was in the practice of selling them publicly, that is a public use which can destroy novelty; a single such sale may commence such a practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts recognize the risk that secret sales for profit could extend practical monopoly beyond the statutory term; sales even for a foreign market may count. Whether a solitary sale suffices depends on circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Piratical use by a confidential recipient does not necessarily defeat patent if inventor acts promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a person confidentially entrusted with knowledge of an invention fraudulently makes it public, the authorities indicate the inventor may obtain a valid patent if he takes immediate steps to give notice of his exclusive right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate assertion and steps to legalize the right (e.g., prompt application, public notice) can preserve patentability despite the fraudulent disclosure by an agent or employee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural requirement in framing novelty/public-use defence: specify parts attacked
rubrics_metrics.description: Care is to be taken in framing this defence to ascertain whether the whole or only a part of the substance of the thing patented is open to the objection and to specify in the notice of defence the particular parts intended to be attacked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is necessary because partial attacks may be met by disclaimers and may affect costs; courts will consider whether the attack goes to the originality of the whole patent (an answer to the action) or only to a part (may only affect costs).
